title: Camping Gourmet: Making Dehydrated Veggie Jerky with a Mandoline
meta_description: Learn how to make crisp dehydrated veggie jerky using a mandoline slicer. Step‑by‑step tips, slice settings, seasoning ideas, and FAQ for tasty, portable snacks
html:
When you’re out on the trail or setting up camp, having a protein‑packed snack that’s lightweight and flavorful makes a huge difference. Using a mandoline to create dehydrated veggie jerky is faster and more consistent than hand‑cutting, and the result is a snack that holds up to any adventure. Below you’ll find the tools, techniques, and seasoning blends that turn ordinary vegetables into gourmet jerky you’ll actually want to eat.

Why a Mandoline Is the Secret Weapon for Dehydrated Veggie Jerky

The key to great jerky is uniform thickness. Thin, even slices dry quickly and develop that coveted chew without turning brittle. A mandoline slicer, especially the Mandoline Slicer with its adjustable blades and hand guard, gives you restaurant‑thin slices in seconds. The precision eliminates guesswork, so you spend less time waiting for the dehydrator and more time enjoying the trail.

Choosing the Right Vegetables

Not all veggies make good jerky. Look for low‑water‑content varieties that can be sliced thin without becoming mushy. Here are my go‑to choices:

  • Carrots – naturally sweet, hold flavor well.
  • Beets – earthy flavor, beautiful color.
  • Zucchini – mild taste, quick to dry.
  • Sweet potatoes – dense texture, great for hearty snacks.
  • Portobello mushroom caps – umami‑rich and slightly chewy.

Wash and dry the produce thoroughly before slicing. Excess moisture will extend drying time and can cause uneven texture.

Setting Up Your Mandoline for Perfect Slices

Start by attaching the appropriate blade on the Mandoline Slicer. For jerky, aim for a 1‑2 mm thickness – the “thin” setting on most models. Secure the hand guard and always use the safety handle; the blade is razor‑sharp and a slip can be dangerous. Place the vegetable on the platform, hold the guard, and glide it smoothly toward the blade. If you’re working with larger items like sweet potatoes, cut them into manageable chunks first.

Marinating and Seasoning the Slices

A good marinade penetrates the thin slices quickly, adding flavor and helping preserve the jerky. Here’s a simple, all‑natural blend that works for any vegetable:

  1. 1/4 cup soy sauce or tamari.
  2. 2 tbsp olive oil.
  3. 1 tbsp maple syrup or honey.
  4. 1 tsp smoked paprika.
  5. ½ tsp garlic powder.
  6. Pinch of black pepper.

Combine the ingredients in a bowl, toss the mandoline‑cut slices, and let them sit for 30‑45 minutes. Because the slices are thin, you’ll notice the flavor infusing almost immediately.

Dehydrating the Slices

Lay the marinated slices in a single layer on your dehydrator trays. Overcrowding traps moisture and leads to uneven drying. Set the dehydrator to 135 °F (57 °C) – the sweet spot for preserving nutrients while achieving that classic jerky chew. Dry times vary by vegetable and slice thickness, but most slices finish in 4‑6 hours. Check for flexibility; the jerky should bend without snapping.

Storing and Using Your Dehydrated Veggie Jerky

Once cooled, store the jerky in airtight bags or vacuum‑sealed pouches. In a cool, dry place it will stay fresh for up to three months. Pack a few strips in your daypack for a quick protein boost, or crumble them over salads for a crunchy garnish. The flavor intensifies after a day or two, so don’t hesitate to let it sit briefly before the first bite.

FAQ

Do I need to pre‑blanch vegetables before slicing?

Blanching is optional. For tough vegetables like carrots or beets, a quick 2‑minute blanch can soften the fibers and speed up drying. For most other veggies, especially mushrooms and zucchini, you can slice and dehydrate directly.

Can I use a regular kitchen knife instead of a mandoline?

You can, but achieving uniform 1‑2 mm slices is labor‑intensive and inconsistent. The mandoline’s adjustable blades give you the precision needed for even dehydration, reducing drying time and improving texture.

Is it safe to eat dehydrated veggie jerky without a formal meat‑free jerky preservative?

Yes. The low water activity achieved by proper dehydration (below 0.6) inhibits bacterial growth. Keeping the jerky dry, refrigerated after opening, and consuming within a few months ensures safety.
